summaries.example: Imagine a story about a treasure chest that could have been painted blue instead of red. The real chest is actual. The blue chest is not actual, but it may be a possible object if the story describes a way things could have been. Philosophers ask whether that blue chest is a real object somewhere, merely described by a representation, or not an object at all.
summaries.summary: Philosophers use the phrase “possible object” for something that could exist, even if it does not exist in the real world. Everyone agrees that actual things are possible, but they disagree about whether non-actual possible things are genuine objects. One view says that all the ways the universe could be are possible worlds, and possible objects belong to those worlds. Another view says possible worlds are actual descriptions or representations of ways things could be. A third family of views, influenced by Alexius Meinong, allows objects that do not exist in the ordinary sense, including some impossible objects. The debate also concerns unicorns, fictional characters, and names for things that do not exist. These questions matter because possible objects help philosophers explain possibility and some results in modal logic.
key_ideas: Every actual object is possible: if something really exists, it could exist.
Some philosophers think there are possible objects that are not actual. Others think these are only descriptions or representations.
Possible-world theories explain possibility by asking how things are in different complete ways the universe could be.
Theories disagree about objects in stories, such as unicorns or Sherlock Holmes. Some story objects may even have conflicting features.
Possible objects are useful in logic, but philosophers still debate how to identify them clearly.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic asks a basic question: what kinds of things are there? It also helps explain words such as “could,” “might,” and “must.” Thinking about possible objects shows that a simple sentence about what could happen may hide difficult questions about existence, identity, stories, and logic.

important_terms.definition: An object that could exist or could have certain features, even if it does not actually exist.
The way things really are, including the objects that really exist.
A complete way the universe could be, including the actual way the universe is.
The view that some objects could exist without actually existing.
The view that everything that exists is actual, while possible worlds are representations of ways things could be.
A made-up object, such as a story character, whose status philosophers debate.

questions_to_think_about: Is a treasure chest that could have existed but never did an object?
Does a story character exist in any sense?
Can two different possible objects look exactly alike?
Why might it be difficult to say which possible object a name refers to?

summaries.example: Consider the claim, “This particular boat could have been built without a small plank.” A possible-world theory must explain what makes the boat in that other situation the same boat, or a counterpart of it. On a counterpart theory, a sufficiently similar boat in another world can make the claim true. On a modal-dimensional view, the very boat may exist across modal dimensions. An actualist may instead represent the alternative situation using actual descriptions or parts. Each approach gains something, but each faces questions about identity and what counts as a genuine object.
summaries.summary: The metaphysics of possible objects begins with a distinction between actuality and possibility. It is uncontroversial that actual objects are possible, but the claim that some possible objects are non-actual divides philosophers. In the possible-worlds framework, modal claims are understood by reference to complete ways reality could be. Possibilist realism treats non-actual worlds and their objects as genuine, while actualist representationism treats worlds as actual representations of possible ways reality could be. Lewis’s modal counterpart theory explains de re possibility through counterparts and analyzes worlds in terms of maximal spatiotemporal wholes. Modal-dimensionalism instead treats objects as persisting through modal dimensions. Both views face identity and specificity problems. Actualist theories face a nesting problem when a possibility inside another possibility must refer back to an object represented within the first. Meinongian approaches avoid some difficulties by allowing non-existent objects, and theories of fictional objects raise related questions about existence, incompleteness, and inconsistency. Possible objects also support important principles in quantified modal logic, although rival approaches question whether the resulting commitments are acceptable.
key_ideas: The central dispute concerns whether non-actual possible objects are genuine objects or whether possible worlds are only actual representations.

Possibilist realism treats non-actual objects as existing in realms comparable to the actual realm. Lewis’s version analyzes worlds as maximal spatiotemporal wholes and uses counterparts for claims about what an object could have been.

Modal-dimensionalism offers a different realist picture: objects may persist through modal dimensions, so counterpart objects are not required. It leaves more of the notion of a possible world unexplained.

Actualist representationism uses actual sentences, propositions, states of affairs, or similar items to represent complete ways things could be. It faces a nesting problem when one possibility refers to an object inside another possibility.

Meinongian theories distinguish existence from a broader status such as subsistence, and may include non-existent or impossible objects. Other theories treat fictional objects as actual abstract objects or as products of make-believe.

The specificity problem affects both realist and representational approaches: descriptions may fail to determine one unique possible object. Possible objects also play a role in validating the Barcan Formula and its converse in quantified modal logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate tests how much metaphysical structure is required to explain ordinary modal language: what could have happened, what must be true, and what might have existed. It connects metaphysics with semantics and logic. It also clarifies why apparently familiar cases—boats, fictional characters, unicorns, or an unactualized object—create difficult questions about identity, reference, and existence.

important_terms.definition: An object that exists in at least one possible way, whether or not it exists in the actual world.
The status of the world as it really is; in possible-world semantics, the actual world is the world representing how things really are.
A complete way reality could be. In modal semantics, possibility is often analyzed by reference to some possible world.
The position that some non-actual possible objects are genuine objects, with existence understood across realms or worlds.
The position that possible worlds are actual representations of ways the universe could be, rather than additional concrete realms.
A theory associated with David Lewis in which an object’s possibilities are explained through suitable counterparts in other possible worlds.
A form of possibilist realism that treats objects as persisting through additional modal dimensions, rather than using counterparts.
The challenge of determining exactly which possible object a name or description identifies, especially when many candidates fit equally well.

questions_to_think_about: If two possible objects have all the same qualities, what could make them different objects?
Does a counterpart in another possible world make it true that you could have acted differently?
Can an actual representation refer to an object that exists only according to that representation?
Should fictional objects be possible objects, actual abstract objects, or neither?
What does the Barcan Formula seem to assume about the range of objects over which we quantify?

summaries.example: Suppose your school plans a science fair. One display is a real model of a robot. Another display shows how the robot could have been built with three wheels instead of four. Is the three-wheeled robot a possible object? One philosopher might say it exists in a different possible world. Another might say it is only an actual description of how the robot could have been. A third might say it is an object that does not exist but has certain features. The example shows why “could have been” can lead to questions about what counts as an object.
summaries.summary: A possible object is something that could exist, even if it does not exist in the actual world. The main disagreement is whether non-actual possible objects are genuine objects. Possibilism says that some such objects exist in other realms or possible worlds. Actualism says that everything that exists is actual; possible worlds are instead actual representations of complete ways reality could have been. Within possibilist realism, Lewis’s counterpart theory explains statements about what an object could have been by using similar objects in other worlds. A different realist view, modal-dimensionalism, says objects can persist through modal dimensions. Both realist views face questions about how possible objects are identified. Actualist theories face a nesting problem when one possible situation refers to an object inside another possible situation. Meinongian theories allow non-existent objects and distinguish existence from a broader kind of objecthood. The same issues appear in discussions of unicorns, fictional characters, and the logical principles used to reason about possibility.
key_ideas: Philosophers agree that actual objects are possible, but they disagree about whether some possible objects are non-actual.
Possible-world theories describe possibility by comparing the actual world with complete ways the universe could have been.
Possibilist realists treat non-actual possible objects as genuine. Actualist representationists treat possible worlds as actual representations, such as sentences or propositions.
Lewis’s counterpart theory says that what you could have done may depend on a similar counterpart of you in another world, rather than you yourself being there.
Some theories allow non-existent objects. They may also allow impossible objects, such as something described as both round and square.

Fictional objects and mythical creatures create special problems because stories may not give enough information to identify one unique object, and stories can sometimes assign conflicting properties.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic helps us see that words like “could,” “might,” and “must” are not just casual expressions. They raise questions about worlds, objects, identity, and language. The debate also connects everyday examples—such as alternative designs or story characters—to formal logic and to larger theories about what exists.

important_terms.definition: Something that could exist or could have certain properties, even if it is not part of the actual world.
The condition of being part of the world as it really is.
A complete way things could be, used to explain claims about possibility and necessity.
The view that some possible objects are real objects even though they are not actual.
The view that everything that exists is actual and that possible worlds are representations of ways things could be.
A theory that explains what an object could have been by referring to a similar counterpart in another possible world.
A problem about deciding exactly which possible object a description or name picks out.
A view, influenced by Meinong, that allows objects that do not exist in the ordinary sense.

questions_to_think_about: Would a different version of you in another possible world be you or only your counterpart?
If a story never says how many hairs a character has, does the character have a definite number?
Can something be an object without existing?
Why might a possible world be understood as a description instead of a place?
What problems arise when a story gives one character incompatible features?
